lede: Weekend edition: week in review and week ahead.
geo_headlines: IRAN OFFERED A SEVEN-DAY PLAN TO REOPEN HORMUZ, AND THE WALL STREET JOURNAL REPORTS TRUMP REJECTED IT. Foreign Minister Araghchi said Tehran conveyed the plan through Qatar: a seven-day halt to hostilities, sanctions and blockade relief, and the strait reopened on day seven. Within hours the Journal, citing US officials, said Trump turned it down and expects renewed bombing is likely. **This landed after Friday's settle**, so the oil market has not priced it yet - Sunday evening's reopen is the first test.

FRIDAY'S BOND MOVE WAS A BULL STEEPENER: THE FRONT END RALLIED AND THE LONG END MADE NEW HIGHS. Treasury's curve file: 2-year 4.81% (-6bp), 10-year 5.17% (-1), 30-year 5.49% (+2) and 20-year 5.54% (+1) - the 20 and 30 at their highest closes of 2026. 2s10s widened to 36bp from 31. Intraday, the 10-year touched about 5.23%, the highest since June 2007 per CNBC, before oil fell and pulled it back.

THE WEEK'S YIELD RISE WAS AGAIN ALMOST ENTIRELY REAL RATES. From 9/18 to 9/25 the nominal 10-year rose 16bp (5.01% to 5.17%) and the real 10-year rose 15bp (2.68% to 2.83%), so the 10-year breakeven moved one basis point, 233 to 234. The market is marking up the price of money, not its inflation forecast.

HIKE ODDS EASED ON FRIDAY AS OIL FELL. CME FedWatch (reporting 9/25): October hike 64.2%, down from 70.9%; at least one hike by December 91.9%, from 93.9%; and a 49.8% chance that December leaves the range 50bp higher than today. Cleveland's Hammack said the biggest risk is that an inflationary mindset sets in and policy must be restrictive.

BUSINESS INVESTMENT IS STRONG AND CONSUMERS ARE GLUM - BOTH CONFIRMED FRIDAY. Durable goods orders were unchanged in August against a forecast drop of about 0.4%, and core capital goods orders jumped 1.6% versus 0.5% expected (Reuters). Michigan's final September sentiment was 48.1, a four-month low, with year-ahead inflation expectations at 4.6% and long-run at 3.4%, up from 3.3%.

STOCKS POSTED A WINNING WEEK, LED BY THE NASDAQ 100. Friday: S&P 500 +0.51% to 7,743.41, Nasdaq 100 +0.42%, Dow +0.93%, semis +1.41%, VIX 14.87. For the week the S&P rose 1.21%, the Nasdaq 100 3.25%, the Dow 0.28% (ending a three-week losing streak). Microsoft +3.66% on new Copilot tools; Meta -3.33% after Thursday's 4.5% jump; Akamai closed +3.20%, giving back most of Thursday's 18.8% after-hours spike.

NEXT WEEK SWAPS LAST WEEK'S BOND SUPPLY FOR A HEAVY DATA CALENDAR. JOLTS and Conference Board confidence Tuesday, August PCE plus the Q2 GDP third estimate Wednesday 8:30, ISM manufacturing Thursday, and the September jobs report Friday 8:30. Governor Barr speaks on the outlook Tuesday and Vice Chair Jefferson Thursday. Micron reports Wednesday after the close.
client_frame_short: A good week for stocks and a hard one for bonds, and the two are more connected than they look. The S&P 500 gained 1.2% and the Nasdaq 100 more than 3%, while the 30-year Treasury yield closed the week at its highest level of the year. Nearly all of the rise in yields came from real rates rather than inflation expectations, which means investors are demanding more to lend, not forecasting runaway prices. **Late Friday, after markets closed, Iran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz was reportedly rejected, so oil may open higher Sunday night.** Nothing here calls for action; next week's inflation and jobs data will matter more than any headline.
client_frame:
The simplest way to describe this week to a client: stocks went up, bonds went down, and both moves came from the same place - a stronger economy that is costing more to finance.

On the equity side, the S&P 500 rose 1.2% for the week to 7,743, the Nasdaq 100 rose 3.25%, and the Dow ended a three-week losing streak. Neither index is at a new high: the S&P is 0.71% below its August 13 record close and the Nasdaq 100 0.40% below its September 22 record. Friday's leaders were Microsoft, up 3.7% on new AI tools, and a broad lift as oil fell.

On the bond side, the 10-year Treasury yield rose 16 basis points for the week to 5.17%, and intraday Friday it touched its highest level since 2007 before easing. The 30-year closed at 5.49%, its highest of 2026. The point worth making to clients is what drove it: the inflation-protected 10-year yield rose 15 of those 16 basis points. The market's implied inflation forecast barely moved. Investors are simply charging more to lend money for ten years.

That fits Friday's data. Orders for business equipment jumped 1.6% in August, triple what economists expected - companies are investing, largely in AI and data centers. Consumers are the soft spot: Michigan sentiment finished September at 48.1, a four-month low, with households expecting 4.6% inflation over the next year. Strong business spending plus anxious households and $100 Brent is a mix that keeps the Fed leaning toward tightening. Futures give about a 64% chance of another hike in October and more than 90% by December, though those odds eased Friday.

The weekend risk is oil. Iran offered a seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and the Wall Street Journal reports the President rejected it. That news arrived after Friday's settle, when Brent had already fallen 2.1% on hopes for a deal. Expect some of that decline to reverse when trading reopens Sunday evening.

The advice stays deliberately steady. Yields above 5% mean high-quality bonds now pay a real return again, which is an opportunity for anyone holding excess cash. Stocks are close to their highs without being euphoric - the VIX closed at 14.87. What would change the view: a 10-year close above 5.25%, or a hot August PCE report on Wednesday that pushes the market to price a third hike.
